item.title: Over 20,000 new homes completed, government still behind target
item.description:
Over 20,000 new homes completed, government still behind target

November 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Builders completed 18,100 new homes in the Netherlands between July and September, about 3,200 more than in the same period last year, according to figures from national statistics office CBS.

Completions were also up 1,600 compared to the second quarter. Counting conversions of offices and other buildings into homes, as well as demolitions and homes lost to renovation, the housing stock grew by 20,300 homes.

The number of building permits issued for new homes dropped sharply to 16,600, after an unusually high 48,900 in the second quarter. Almost 30,000 of those were issued in June alone. CBS said this was because local authorities rushed to register permits before new rules on grid congestion came into force.

As a result, the number of homes that have permits but have not yet been built fell  by 1,400 to around 257,000. CBS said more homes have been given permits than have been built in recent years.

The value of permitted housing construction was €3 billion in the quarter, 19% lower than a year earlier.

Construction firms’ turnover rose 5.7% year on year, the third quarterly rise in a row. But 163 construction firms went bankrupt in the quarter, 30 more than in the previous three months.

The cabinet wants 100,000 homes to be added each year to tackle the housing shortage. That works out at 25,000 a quarter, around 5,000 more than were added between July and September.

item.title: Dutch embassy hit in Kyiv as Putin vows Crimea bridge revenge
item.description:
Dutch embassy hit in Kyiv as Putin vows Crimea bridge revenge

November 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch embassy in Kyiv was hit during drone strikes on Thursday afternoon, damaging the building and surrounding area, though no one was reported harmed. Shortly thereafter, Russian president Putin pledged to respond to recent attacks on the Crimean bridge, which the Netherlands was involved in.

“Fortunately our colleagues are unharmed, though there is minor damage to the building,” Dutch foreign minister Tom Berendsen said. He said the ministry was looking into exactly what had happened and that its priority now was the wellbeing of its staff.

The Kyiv Independent reported that the projectile was a Russian drone which crashed close to the embassy, damaging cars and a security post and shattering windows in the building, during an hours-long attack on the capital. The site said it was not clear whether the drone had been aimed at the area around the embassy or had been shot down.

Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said Russian attacks on Kyiv had once again damaged a diplomatic mission, broadcaster NOS reported. Ukrainian media also reported Russian drone attacks throughout the day, with air raid sirens sounding several times in the capital.

Crimean bridge attack 
The strike comes two days after a Ukrainian attack on the Kerch bridge to Crimea, which Dutch arms maker Destinus publicly said it had been involved in. Destinus said seven of its Ruta missiles had hit the bridge and that it was “proud to support the Ukrainian army”.

On Wednesday, Russia’s embassy in The Hague said Moscow had been informed of Dutch involvement and asked whether The Hague was “openly taking part in the conflict”.

Berendsen told MPs that Russian embassies were being used to spread the Kremlin’s narrative. “They want to drive a wedge between us, so we have to see it through that lens,” he said.

In April, Russia’s defence ministry put a Destinus factory on a list of potential targets, which former Russian president Dmitry Medvedev said should be taken “literally”, NOS and other outlets reported.

Staff in Ukraine
On Thursday morning, NRC reported that Destinus employees had personally shot down Russian drones in Ukraine and helped the Ukrainian army launch attacks towards Russia.

The defence ministry told the paper that using a weapon system against a party in an armed conflict counts as direct participation in hostilities.

Destinus denies carrying out military operations and says it only provided technical support. Defence minister Dilan Yeşilgöz has declined to comment on NRC’s findings.

Experts told NOS that by going public, Destinus could increase the risk of Russian sabotage or cyberattacks against it. “We know that Russia has gone after companies like this in Europe,” missile expert Fabian Hoffmann said. Defence analyst Patrick Bolder said the company was already on a Russian list of targets “and would not easily come off it”.

Deze middag is een projectiel ingeslagen achter de Nederlandse ambassade in Kyiv. Onze collega’s zijn gelukkig ongedeerd, er is wel lichte schade aan het gebouw. We onderzoeken wat er exact is gebeurd. Onze prioriteit ligt nu bij het welzijn van onze medewerkers.

— Tom Berendsen (@ministerBZ) November 19, 2026

item.title: Prostate cancer surgeries improving: fewer men left incontinent
item.description:
Prostate cancer surgeries improving: fewer men left incontinent

November 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The share of men who end up incontinent after having a prostate tumour removed has roughly halved over the past few years, broadcaster NOS reports.

Until 2020, about 30% of patients in the Netherlands who got the operation were left incontinent afterwards. Between 2022 and 2024 that fell to 14%, according to insurers’ data analysed by the quality registry Dutch Prostate Audit.

Prostate cancer is the most common cancer among men in the Netherlands. Just over 16,000 men were diagnosed with it last year, and it killed 3,334 in 2024, according to CBS figures.

There has been a huge gap in outcomes between the hospitals that do the surgeries, which has also narrowed a lot in recent years.

A PhD study looking at operations between 2016 to 2020 found that one hospital had a 19% rate of causing incontinence by the operation and another 85%. Now the differences go from about 10% to 25% at most.

“That was hard to face, and it forced urologists in the Netherlands to work together more on improving things,” Rik Somford, a urologist at the Canisius-Wilhelmina hospital in Nijmegen who chairs the working group behind the push, told NOS.

Patients still can’t see how individual hospitals perform, and people want more transparency. Next year hospitals will start publishing some results, including complications within 90 days, whether the cancer was fully removed and whether patients are still incontinent a year later.

item.title: UN court in The Hague rules Myanmar committed genocide
item.description:
UN court in The Hague rules Myanmar committed genocide

November 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority. It is the first time the UN’s highest court has found a state responsible for committing genocide.

Reading the judgment at the Peace Palace, court president Yuji Iwasawa said the court was “fully convinced” that Myanmar’s security forces had acted with the intent to destroy “a substantial part” of the Rohingya population during a military crackdown in 2017.

The court found that soldiers killed thousands of Rohingya civilians (around 10,000, according to the evidence), committed widespread sexual violence and violence against children, and attacked people as they fled to neighbouring Bangladesh. More than 730,000 Rohingya crossed the border.

The case was brought in 2019 by The Gambia, with the backing of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. The Netherlands and Canada said in 2020 that they would intervene in support.

Myanmar has always denied genocide. It says the operation targeted Rohingya militants who had attacked police posts.

The ICJ settles disputes between states and is separate from the International Criminal Court (ICC), which is also in The Hague and prosecutes individuals. Its rulings are final and cannot be appealed, but the court has no way of enforcing them.

The ruling could also affect South Africa’s genocide case against Israel, which is still before the court, the Volkskrant reported. The judges said other motives, such as fighting an insurgency, do not rule out genocidal intent. But they kept the bar high: genocide has to be the only reasonable conclusion from the evidence as a whole.

item.title: 1,100 new poplars to save historic tree-lined Maas riverbanks
item.description:
1,100 new poplars to save historic tree-lined Maas riverbanks

November 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Some 1,100 new poplars are being planted along the river Maas to preserve the rows of trees that have lined both banks for almost a century, broadcaster NOS reported.

The trees, which stand 110 metres apart between Boxmeer and Geertruidenberg, were once used by skippers to navigate river. They are known as beacon trees (bakenbomen) and have become a defining part of the river landscape.

Many of the original trees are reaching the end of their lives, and for years dead trees were not replaced. Only 700 are left. The replanting will bring the total to 1,800 over the coming years.

The national government, the provinces of Noord Brabant, Gelderland, and Limburg, and 14 local authorities along the river are putting €4.6 million into the project.

They signed the agreement on national tree day (Boomfeestdag) and have committed to paying for maintenance for the next 100 years. North Brabant will coordinate the work. A network of volunteers and civic groups is also involved.

The new trees are black poplars, which the provinces describe as native to the Maas valley and good for biodiversity and nature restoration.

item.title: Corporations build 24,000 social homes, say state help needed
item.description:
Corporations build 24,000 social homes, say state help needed

November 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch housing corporations built almost 24,000 new social rent homes last year, but say they cannot keep up the pace without more help from the government.

Some 10,000 homes were lost to demolition and sales, giving a net increase of 13,000, broadcaster NOS reported, based on the annual report from housing corporation association Aedes. Corporations built 2,100 more social rent homes than a year earlier.

There are now 2.1 million social rent homes in the Netherlands. For new contracts, the rent on a social housing property can be no more than €932.93 a month.

Homes renting for up to €1,228.07 count as mid-market rentals, which corporations also build. Many corporation homes now have an energy label of A or better.

However, corporations are still spending more on each home than they take in in rent. Aedes puts the average shortfall at €44 per home, down from €48 a year earlier. Most of that improvement comes from higher rents and from selling homes. Corporations borrow to fund 52% of their investments.

“We know that this way of working cannot go on,” Aedes chair Liesbeth Spies said. Without new measures, corporations will face “painful choices between new construction, maintenance and liveability”, she said.

The cabinet plans to cut a tax paid by housing corporations from 2028. Aedes says higher interest rates and rising costs will swallow up the extra money.

item.title: FVD expels two members after neo-Nazi cage fight exposé
item.description:
FVD expels two members after neo-Nazi cage fight exposé

November 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The far-right Forum for Democracy (FVD) has expelled two members and pushed a Den Bosch councillor to step down. The move follows a TV investigation that linked people in and around the party to a neo-Nazi network that organises illegal cage fights.

The investigation was done by current affairs programme Zembla and Flemish broadcaster VRT’s Pano, using an undercover infiltrator and hidden cameras.

This summer Zembla filmed Ramon van Asch, who led FVD’s group on Den Bosch council, leaving a cage fight in Oeffelt, North Brabant, with a baby in his arms.

Fighters and spectators repeatedly gave the Nazi salute. Van Asch said an acquaintance had invited him and that he went home once the fighting began.

Hitler commemoration
Two members of FVD’s youth wing fought at another event in Finsterwolde, Groningen, according to Zembla. One of them, Luc Kluytmans, is one of the two members the party has now expelled.

He was also secretly filmed in April at a Hitler commemoration in Luxembourg, run by the neo-Nazi group Wolvenrad, where he took part in burning books by Jewish writers.

In a statement on social media, FVD said “unacceptable behaviour and views” had been shown at the fight. It said it had asked Van Asch to step down and that he had done so.

“Not problematic”
Ralf Dekker, who leads FVD’s MPs, was less concerned when NOS showed him the footage. “Everyone should go where they want,” he said. “I don’t find that problematic at all.” He later said he had not known about the report when he was asked, although Zembla had already approached the party for comment.

The counter-terrorism coordinator NCTV says fights of this kind are meant to strengthen the “white race” physically. It says they pose no violent threat in the Netherlands for now, but could make violence more likely.

Ahead of March’s local elections, several FVD candidates were found to have links to extremist organisations. FVD leader Lidewij de Vos called their past activities “youthful indiscretions”.

The documentary is on NPO 2 tonight.

Nieuws | Geheime beelden in bezit van Zembla leggen verregaande connecties bloot tussen een neonazi-netwerk en Forum voor Democratie. Op beelden van illegale vechttoernooien zie je neonazi’s die elkaar knock-out slaan en de Hitler-groet brengen. Onder de aanwezigen ontdekken wij leden van beruchte neonazi-groepen, veroordeelde extremisten en leden van FVD. Het gaat onder meer om prominent partijlid Ramon van Asch, fractievoorzitter voor de FVD in Den Bosch.

— Zembla (@ZEMBLA) November 18, 2026

item.title: Regional bus and train strikes return on Monday and Tuesday
item.description:
Regional bus and train strikes return on Monday and Tuesday

November 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Regional bus and train drivers across the Netherlands will strike on Monday and Tuesday, after union members rejected employers’ final offer for a new pay and conditions deal.

The FNV and CNV unions say more strikes will follow on December 3, 4, 14, 15 and 18 if the two-day walkout does not move employers, Het Parool reported.

Some 13,000 workers, mainly bus drivers, are covered by the public transport collective agreement, which expired on July 1. Staff at Arriva, Transdev, EBS, Qbuzz, Keolis and RET’s regional services are involved. City transport in Amsterdam, Rotterdam and The Hague is not affected.

The unions held a first nationwide 24-hour strike on October 14. They had planned to strike one day a week until Christmas, but suspended the strike after the employers’ organisation VWOV made a number of commitments and talks resumed.

The talks ended with the VWOV putting a final offer on the table. The employers said it allowed for pay rises while taking into account “the financial limits of our sector”. A large majority of FNV and CNV members voted against it.

The unions say pay is not the problem. They object to employers’ plans to raise the starting age of a scheme for workers over 50 to 53, and to cut the allowance for working irregular hours.

item.title: Dutch arms maker’s staff hunted Russian drones in Ukraine: NRC
item.description:
Dutch arms maker’s staff hunted Russian drones in Ukraine: NRC

November 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Employees of Dutch arms manufacturer Destinus have been actively participating in the Ukraine war, engaging in drone battles with Russian forces, according to an investigation by NRC.

The defence ministry says such actions amount to direct participation in hostilities, and experts warn the company’s activities could drag the Netherlands into the war.

On Tuesday, the company publicly announced its missiles had been used in a specific attack, the strike on the Crimea bridge. It has now confirmed to NRC that its staff “launched and operated” interceptor drones against incoming Russian attack drones, without live explosives and under the direction of Ukrainian soldiers.

NRC asked the defence ministry whether Destinus employees are allowed to use weapons against Russian drones or targets. The ministry said that launching or operating a weapons system counts as taking part in the fighting, and that anyone who does so loses the protection given to civilians under the laws of war. Explaining to soldiers how a system works does not, it said.

Legal risk

Jessica Dorsey, an international law lecturer at Utrecht University, said company employees who take a direct part in fighting can be treated as targets, and the Ukrainian army’s consent makes no difference. Liesbeth Zegveld, a professor of the law of war, said they could also face prosecution.

Zegveld also told NRC that the company could drag the Netherlands into the war. “The formal position is that the Netherlands is not at war,” she said. “But by supporting companies that take part in this way, you muddle your way into the war.”

Wimar Bolhuis, a left-wing PRO MP who sits on parliament’s defence committee, called the findings “worrying” and has asked the Defence ministry to explain how the drones were tested and how the export licences were granted. “We need to know what is really happening there,” he said. Volt leader Laurens Dassen also called for an investigation into whether Destinus lets staff take part in the war.

Battle testing
NRC spoke to more than 40 people, including current and former employees, investors and advisers, and drew on internal documents, messages and video. It found that from autumn 2024, a Destinus team in Ukraine tested the company’s Hornet interceptor drone against Russian-made Shahed drones, using drones shipped from the Netherlands.

Internal messages seen by NRC show that the drones crashed repeatedly, and one was nearly lost over a village. When the Ukrainian army asked whether the drone was ready for use, the team on the ground said it was not ready for combat missions. A team leader in Spain pushed for it to fly anyway.

Kokorich told NRC he did not recognise its descriptions of chaotic factories, of the drones’ poor condition or of a start-up mentality at the company, and said safety is “of the utmost importance” at Destinus.

Strike on Voronezh
NRC also reported that in June 2023, before Destinus moved its military arm to the Netherlands, employees went to the front near Kharkiv to test the company’s first attack drones. The aircraft carried explosives and were set to hit a military airfield near the Russian city of Voronezh, 180 kilometres across the border. According to the paper, Destinus staff were closely involved.

On the morning of June 9, a drone hit an apartment block in Voronezh and three people were injured. NRC said employees who saw footage of the strike suspected the drone was theirs, though it cannot be said with certainty where the Destinus drone came down.

Destinus said the Ukrainian army selects targets and decides on military operations, and the company provides “technical support in line with its contracts”. “Destinus does not carry out military operations,” it said.

Government backing
Destinus was founded in Switzerland in 2021 by Russian-born Kokorich and registered its military arm in Hengelo in 2024. In 2024 he settled US fraud charges over his previous space company, without admitting or denying them, and paid a $2 million penalty and accepted a five-year ban from running listed companies.

The Netherlands has since become a key customer. In June it agreed to pay for 700 Ruta cruise missiles for Ukraine, worth €250 million, a package the cabinet first described as drones.

In August, the defence ministry signed a contract with Destinus to develop a navy version of the Hornet, part of a project budgeted at €250 million to €1 billion.

The foreign ministry, which grants arms export licences for Ukraine, told NRC that manufacturers are responsible for safety defects and Ukraine is responsible for assessing the quality of the weapons.

On Wednesday, the Russian embassy asked whether the Netherlands was becoming involved in the war after the Crimea bridge strike. In a parliamentary committee debate on Wednesday, foreign minister Tom Berendsen said his ministry had no further details of Destinus’ role in the bridge attack. He said Russian statements of this kind are intended to sow division and stoke fear.

item.title: Government struggling to reclaim €1.2bn in assets from criminals
item.description:
Government struggling to reclaim €1.2bn in assets from criminals

November 18, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch government has an outstanding bill of €1.2 billion in unclaimed proceeds of crime and compensation payments, according to figures from the agency responsible for collecting the money.

The CJIB, the justice department’s debt collection service, said it was struggling to pursue criminals for amounts they owe under court orders designed to prevent them gaining financially.

Proceeds of crime account for two-thirds of the total amount, with 2% of the criminals responsible for 50% of the unpaid debts.

They include “Bolle Jos” Leijdekkers, the drugs baron who is believed to be hiding out in Sierra Leone and is the subject of a €2 million reward for information leading to his capture. He has been ordered to pay the Dutch state a total of €96 million.

“In general these are people who don’t want to pay,” Johan Bac, managing director of the CJIB, told Nieuwsuur. “Their fortune is often concealed by all kinds of international constructions. Tracking it down is very labour-intensive.”

Last year the CJIB managed to seize just €50 million in criminal assets, but the agency warns that the backlog will grow unless it is takes on staff, increases its expertise and can get its hands on criminal assets earlier.

The remaining €500 million consists of payments to victims of a wide range of crimes, €150 million of which has been paid out by the CJIB but still has to be reclaimed.

The agency says this amount is also likely to increase under plans to widen the range of offences for which the government covers the compensation payments, to include crimes such as arson and causing traffic deaths.
